name: Metacognitive Strategies
headline: Effective teachers use metacognitive strategies to help students develop awareness of their own learning, to self-regulate, and to sustain their motivation to learn.
inContext: The trap is treating metacognition as reflection sheets stapled to the end of a practical. The HITS document is precise about what actually matters: students need a repertoire of strategies, they need to be able to select between them, and the advantage of each strategy must be clear to them. That is a year-long build, not a lesson. Science is a good vehicle because it supplies constant, honest feedback on whether a strategy worked — a prediction is wrong, an anomaly appears, a confident answer turns out to be a misconception. The single highest-value move is calibration: making the gap between how well students think they understand and how well they do understand visible to them.

exemplar.problem: Asked how they studied, almost every student described re-reading notes. Confidence surveys before topic tests bore little relationship to results, and students who performed poorly were frequently the most confident — they had no way of knowing what they did not know.

phases.label: Build the repertoire
phases.what: Three strategies are taught explicitly, with their evidence and with when each is useful.
phases.detail: Retrieval practice, self-explanation, and concept mapping — taught as content, modelled, and practised on real science. Students are told why each works and where it is the wrong choice, because the HITS document is clear that the advantage of a strategy must be clear to students or they will not select it. Re-reading is discussed honestly as the strategy that feels most effective and is among the least.

phases.label: Calibrate
phases.what: Students predict their score before every topic test and compare it afterwards — repeatedly.
phases.detail: The object of discussion is the gap, not the mark. Over-confidence, once it has been visible three or four times, stops being an argument the teacher has to make. Students who predicted 80% and scored 55% have direct evidence that their monitoring is unreliable, which is the precondition for changing strategy. This costs two minutes per test and is the highest-yield element of the year.

phases.label: Select and monitor
phases.what: For each new topic students choose a strategy, justify the choice against the task, and review whether it worked.
phases.detail: The justification is the assessable part: 'this topic is mostly relationships between processes, so a concept map suits it better than flashcards' shows selection; 'I'll use flashcards because I like them' does not. Concept maps are drawn at the start and end of each focus area so students can see their own model change — which is also a memorable demonstration that understanding is constructed rather than received.

phases.label: Withdraw the scaffolding
phases.what: Students plan, monitor and evaluate their own revision, with teacher prompts deliberately removed.
phases.detail: Checklists and prompts that have been in place all year are withdrawn on a stated schedule. The test of the year's work is not whether students use a strategy when prompted but whether they use one when not. For students moving into Stage 6, this is the capability that determines whether they can manage a depth study and two years of accumulating content.

exemplar.impact: Calibration data across four testing points — the mean absolute gap between predicted and actual scores should narrow, and it is a clean, quantitative measure of a capability that usually gets described only in adjectives. Alongside it, the strategy-choice justifications were coded for whether they referred to the demands of the task or only to preference.

transfer.label: Stage 6 · Investigating Science or any depth study
transfer.text: The same calibration move applied to an extended investigation: students predict which section of their report will score lowest before submission. Students whose prediction is accurate have functioning self-monitoring even if the work is weak, and that distinction changes what the teacher does next — a knowledge problem and a monitoring problem need different responses.

teacher: Teaches specific strategies explicitly, including why and when each one works
Makes the advantage of each strategy clear rather than assuming students will infer it
Builds calibration in — predictions compared against performance, repeatedly
Requires students to justify a strategy choice against the demands of the task
Withdraws prompts and checklists on a stated schedule rather than indefinitely
notDemonstrated: Students are given a choice of activities but never taught how to choose
Reflection is a sheet completed after the task with no bearing on the next one
Metacognitive strategies are taught once and never revisited or transferred
Students are told to 'revise' with no strategy named
The teacher does not encourage students to take responsibility for their own learning
student: Have a repertoire of strategies and select one appropriate to the goal
Reflect on their learning processes and acknowledge the effect of effort
Actively seek feedback because they value it as information about how they learn
Take proactive control of their own learning, and their confidence matches their performance

continuum.label: Emerging
continuum.text: Teachers encourage students to be self-reflective and emphasise that the ability to learn is not fixed.

continuum.label: Evolving
continuum.text: Teachers introduce differentiated strategies, explain how to make informed choices about which to use, and teach students to reflect on and monitor their learning.

continuum.label: Embedding
continuum.text: Teachers explicitly teach several strategies, model their use, embed them in routines and lesson structure, and support students to plan, monitor and evaluate their learning.

continuum.label: Excelling
continuum.text: Strategies are explicitly taught, extensively modelled, embedded in routines, and linked to the content being taught. Students set and monitor their own goals and develop strategies for reaching them.

evidence: Hattie (2009): metacognitive strategies 0.69, self-questioning 0.64, concept mapping 0.64, study skills 0.60, teaching problem solving 0.63; Evidence for Learning: metacognition and self-regulation +8 months.
